failure_mechanism.before: MemoryIndex._load swallowed parse/shape errors and initialized an empty in-memory list; a subsequent add could persist the empty list plus one new entry over the previous index.
failure_mechanism.counterfactual: If a corrupt or malformed index had been followed by a successful add, the complete previously persisted index could have been overwritten.
failure_mechanism.potential_scope: The whole active memory_index.json, including all records present at the verified snapshot.

change: Corrupt or malformed MemoryIndex files now fail closed and are not rewritten as empty.
MemoryIndex writes now use a same-directory fsynced temporary file and atomic replace; a failed save rolls back the in-memory append.
SelfHealing now inspects the canonical runtime memory path and refuses automatic empty-index reconstruction.
Candidate Kernel imports preserve source time and anchors and avoid merging unrelated same-title records.

painful_review.direct_cost_confirmed: No production data loss was observed; the real source remained unchanged during the rehearsal.
painful_review.counterfactual_cost: A later write after a corrupt load could have replaced thousands of private records with an empty index plus the new entry.
painful_review.impact_scope: One runtime memory index and all data consumers depending on it; the rehearsal baseline contained 6979 private records.
painful_review.recurrence_risk_after_change: Silent empty fallback and torn-file writes are covered by fail-closed, atomic-write, and preservation tests. An externally corrupted startup still requires a verified restore point; no stale backup is restored automatically.
painful_review.reusable_lesson: Persistent memory corruption must never be translated into a healthy empty store; recovery must verify a snapshot before replacing any source.
unknowns: No independently labelled real retrieval A/B set has been validated.
No production maintenance-window backend cutover or rollback has been executed.
